explication:
<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, DocuSeal is a full-stack Ruby on Rails web application with a rich client-side layer (using JavaScript, Vue components, and more) to support digital document filling/signing. Its purpose is to allow users to build PDF forms, fill and sign documents online (with features like WYSIWYG PDF form builders, multiple submitters, email notifications, cloud storage integrations, etc.). To capture the overall system in a design diagram, we suggest breaking it into the following components and layers:

1. Frontend (User Interface & Client-side Interactions):
   - Box “User Interface”: Represent browsers and mobile devices accessing the web.
   - Within it, note that the views (app/views) and JavaScript assets (app/javascript) form the primary UI layer. Highlight that there are several specialized JavaScript modules, Vue components (under app/javascript/submission_form and app/javascript/template_builder), and CSS (SCSS) files that render interactive PDF forms.
   - Mark API endpoints consumption by the frontend—for signing, submissions, user profiles, etc.

2. Backend (Rails Web Server & Controllers):
   - Box “Rails Backend”: Show the Ruby on Rails application handling business logic.
   - Indicate two major sub-components:
     a. Traditional HTML controllers (in app/controllers) for normal page rendering (e.g., Dashboard, Setup, Profile, etc.).
     b. API Controllers (in app/controllers/api/*) for handling AJAX and external API requests.
   - Point out that the middleware (Rack, custom middlewares like the one in lib/normalize_client_ip_middleware.rb) sits within this layer.

3. Business Logic, Models, and Libraries:
   - Box “Business & Domain Logic”: Include the Models (app/models) for accounts, submissions, templates, users, and so on.
   - Include “Library / Service Layer”: Represent the lib/ directory items (for PDF processing, template handling, validations, webhook sending, etc.). This group encapsulates complex business logic such as generating PDFs, processing submission events, and validating inputs.

4. Background Processing:
   - Box “Background Jobs” with Sidekiq integration (see config/initializers/sidekiq.rb and app/jobs). Indicate jobs for sending emails and webhooks (jobs in app/jobs such as send_template_created_webhook_request_job.rb, etc.) and other asynchronous tasks like generating previews and handling submissions.
   - Use an arrow showing that the Rails application enqueues tasks to Sidekiq, which in turn interacts with external services (e.g., SMTP, file generation).

5. Persistence and External Integrations:
   - Box “Database & Storage”: Represent the relational database (configured via config/database.yml and migrations in db/migrate) that stores user data, submissions, templates, etc.
   - Also mention external storage options (disk, AWS S3, Google Cloud, Azure) that are configured via app/views/storage_settings and related configuration files.
   - Box “External Services & APIs”: Draw smaller boxes or callouts for:
       • SMTP servers (for ActionMailer-based email communications)
       • Cloud services (for file storage)
       • Webhook endpoints integration (see lib/webhook_urls.rb, controllers for webhook settings)
       • Possibly integrations with SSO/SAML or SMS services (based on Pro features mentioned in the README).

6. Deployment and Containerization:
   - Box “Deployment Environment”: Show that the application is containerized using Docker (Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml) and can be deployed on services like Heroku, Railway, DigitalOcean, etc.
   - Note that the Procfile and configuration under .github/workflows indicate CI/CD and deployment pipelines.
   - Optionally, include a “Load Balancer / Reverse Proxy” or a “Web Server Layer” (if using Puma and/or Caddy for SSL in the Docker Compose deployment) that routes incoming HTTP/HTTPS traffic to the Rails application.

Guidelines for Drawing the Diagram:
• Use clear, labeled boxes for each main component (Frontend, Backend, Business Logic, Background Jobs, Database, and External Services). 
• Inside the “Backend” box, you might subdivide into “HTML Controllers” vs. “API Controllers” (or even illustrate key submodules like Authentication/Devise, document signing flows, etc.).
• Draw directional arrows to represent data flow:
   - From the User Interface (browser/mobile) sending HTTP requests to the Rails Backend.
   - From Rails to the Database (for CRUD operations).
   - From Rails to Background Jobs (via Sidekiq) for asynchronous processing.
   - From Rails outwards to External Services (SMTP, cloud storage, webhooks).
• Apply different colors or shapes to differentiate layers:
   - UI/Client layer could use one color.
   - Backend components may be another color.
   - External integrations and secondary services (like database and cloud storage) might use another style.
• Be sure to include configuration/operational components like Docker/CI pipelines as part of the deployment/execution diagram.

By capturing these detailed elements—especially the separation between the user’s frontend interactions, the web server’s controllers/service layer, the asynchronous background jobs, and the persistence/external integration—you will have a comprehensive and accurate architectural view of DocuSeal that aligns with its purpose as an open-source document filling and signing platform.
</explanation>
